extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, theorems, and practical tests about pushforwards/cohomology, base change, coherence, embeddings, and line-bundle properties on schemes and (especially) projective curves. Intended to guide checking when morphisms are embeddings and when line bundles give maps/embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing of higher pushforwards for affine morphisms (18.8.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π is affine, then for i > 0, R^i π_* F = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an 'easy exercise' remark: the higher direct images of a quasicoherent sheaf under an affine morphism vanish. Use when checking cohomology behavior on affines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural base-change morphism for higher pushforwards (18.8.B(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Cartesian square with π : X → Y and ψ : Z → Y and the pullback diagram, there is a natural morphism ψ^*(R^i π_* F) → R^i π'_* (ψ'^* F) of sheaves on Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: compare the i=0 case to the push-pull formula; construction essentially uses functoriality and the FHHF theorem (Exercise 1.6.H). This describes how higher pushforwards naturally relate under base change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology commutes with affine flat base change (18.8.B(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If ψ : Z → Y is an affine morphism and locally over a cover Spec A_i of Y the pullbacks are Spec B_i with B_i flat over A_i, then the natural morphism ψ^*(R^i π_* F) → R^i π'_* (ψ'^* F) is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes earlier special cases (Exercise 18.2.H). Use flatness (so - ⊗_{A_i} B_i is exact) to get isomorphism; this is the usual affine flat base-change theorem for cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of the base-change map without Cartesian hypothesis (18.8.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can construct the map appearing in 18.8.B(a) without assuming the diagram is Cartesian, provided π' is quasicompact and separated (so R^i π'_* is defined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction arises naturally from the Leray spectral sequence; use Exercise 18.8.B(a) as input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiberwise base-change map to cohomology of fiber (18.8.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: For q ∈ Y there is a natural morphism (R^i π_* F) ⊗ κ(q) → H^i(π^{-1}(q), F|_{π^{-1}(q)}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the fiber of the higher direct image need not equal the cohomology of the fiber, but there is always a natural map; in good situations (cohomology and base change) this map is an isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for higher direct images (18.8.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural morphism (R^i π_* F) ⊗ G → R^i π_* (F ⊗ π^* G) for F on X and G on Y; if G is locally free, this morphism is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use the FHHF theorem. Part (b) emphasizes the common useful special case when G is locally free, giving a clean projection formula for higher pushforwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative dimensional cohomology vanishing (Theorem 18.8.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is projective and Y is locally Noetherian (or O_Y is coherent over itself), then R^i π_* F = 0 for i greater than the maximum dimension of the fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is local on Y; reduce to affine case and cover fibers by m+1 affines to get vanishing above m. This fails without projectivity (see Exercise 18.8.F). Use when bounding nonvanishing degrees of higher direct images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample to relative vanishing without projectivity (18.8.F)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of relative dimensional cohomology vanishing is false without the projective hypothesis; e.g., the open embedding A^n \\ {0} → A^n yields nonvanishing R^{n-1} π_* O_{A^n\{0}}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do the direct cohomology calculation to see the failure; emphasizes necessity of projectivity in Theorem 18.8.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Serre vanishing (18.8.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is proper with Y Noetherian and L is π-ample, then for any coherent F on X there exists m_0 such that for m ≥ m_0, R^i π_* (F ⊗ L^{⊗ m}) = 0 for all i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes Serre vanishing to the relative/proper setting; use ampleness of L and Noetherian hypotheses to kill higher cohomology after twisting sufficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck's Coherence Theorem (18.9.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a proper morphism of locally Noetherian schemes and F is coherent on X, then R^i π_* F is coherent on Y for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Chow's Lemma and the Leray spectral sequence; approach by induction on dim Supp F and reduce to the projective case, then use spectral sequence bookkeeping to conclude coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chow's Lemma (18.9.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : X → Spec A proper with X Noetherian, there exists µ : X' → X surjective and projective such that µ is an isomorphism over a dense open subset of X; hence X admits a projective surjective cover X' birational to X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction proceeds by covering X by affines Ui, embedding them, taking scheme-theoretic closures and a diagonal embedding; useful to reduce proper to projective arguments (e.g., coherence). Several variants and weakenings exist (see exercises/remarks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: injective on closed points + tangent vectors ⇒ closed embedding (19.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is algebraically closed and π : X → Y is projective and finite type, and π is injective on closed points and injective on tangent vectors at closed points, then π is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: over alg. closed fields injectivity on tangent vectors at closed points is equivalent to unramified. The projectivity hypothesis is necessary (counterexample provided). Reduce to finite morphism case (Theorem 19.1.2) to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism of degree 0 or 1 everywhere is a closed embedding (19.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is finite with Y Noetherian and the degree of π at every point of Y is 0 or 1, then π is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof in affine coordinates: show B → A is surjective by Nakayama after localizing at maximal ideals; degree conditions imply cokernel localizations vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective + finite fibers ⇒ finite morphism (reduction used in 19.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π is projective and has finite fibers (fiber dimension 0 everywhere), then π is finite (Theorem 18.1.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use upper semicontinuity of fiber dimension to deduce finiteness of all fibers from closed-point behavior; then apply finiteness criterion to reduce to Theorem 19.1.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality on a curve (19.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a geometrically irreducible regular genus g curve C over a field k there is an invertible sheaf ω_C of degree 2g−2 such that for any coherent F on C, h^i(C, F) = h^{1−i}(C, ω_C ⊗ F^∨) (duality between cohomology groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Serre duality to translate statements about low-degree line bundles into statements about high-degree ones; ω_C has degree 2g−2 and g sections in certain contexts (Exercise references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-degree line bundles have no nonzero sections (19.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L < 0 on a projective regular integral curve C then h^0(C, L) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: any rational section has zeros minus poles equal to deg L; a regular (no poles) section would force deg L ≥ 0. Useful to rule out sections in Riemann-Roch arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 0 line bundles: h^0 equals 0 or 1; trivial iff h^0 = 1 (19.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L = 0 then h^0(C, L) is 0 or 1; if h^0 = 1 then L ≅ O_C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nonzero section with degree 0 has neither zeros nor poles so gives a trivialization. Use geometric integrality (or base change) to ensure h^0(O)=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann-Roch count for large degree (19.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L > 2g−2 then h^0(C, L) = deg L − g + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Serre duality: ω_C ⊗ L^∨ has negative degree so has no sections; combine with Riemann-Roch formula to obtain the stated count. Remember this for dimension counts of linear series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting by a rational point changes h^0 by at most 1 (19.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed point p of degree 1, h^0(C, L) − h^0(C, L(−p)) is 0 or 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact sequence 0 → L(−p) → L → L|_p → 0 and h^0(L|_p)=1 give the bound. Repeat for multiple points to bound drops in h^0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical criterion for base-point-freeness (19.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is alg. closed and for every closed point p, h^0(C, L) − h^0(C, L(−p)) = 1, then L is base-point-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: for each p there exists a section not vanishing at p, so no base points; then L induces a morphism to projective space (Theorem 16.4.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for separating points (19.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for distinct closed points p,q one has h^0(C, L) − h^0(C, L(−p−q)) = 2 then the linear series |L| separates p and q (the induced map separates the images of p and q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equality forces existence of sections vanishing at one point but not the other; use to check injectivity on points of the induced morphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for separating tangent vectors (19.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for a closed point p, h^0(C, L) − h^0(C, L(−2p)) = 2 then the map associated to L separates tangent vectors at p (i.e., is immersive at p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One needs a section vanishing at p to order exactly 1; this gives a local function pulling back with first-order zero but not second, hence nonzero differential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very-ampleness criterion via 2-point tests (19.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for all closed points p and q (possibly equal) one has h^0(C, L) − h^0(C, L(−p−q)) = 2, then L gives a closed embedding (very ample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines separation of points and tangent vectors; with Theorem 19.1.1 this ensures the induced map is a closed embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree bounds for base-point-freeness and very-ampleness (19.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve C over an algebraically closed field: if deg L ≥ 2g then L is base-point-free; if deg L ≥ 2g+1 then L is very ample (gives a closed embedding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior numerical results and Riemann-Roch to show h^0 behavior and the 2-point/tangent separation conditions. Remember these standard degree thresholds for curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness criterion on curves (19.2.C / 19.2.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a projective, regular, integral curve over k (geometrically regular/integral), an invertible sheaf L is ample if and only if deg L > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a purely numerical ampleness test on curves; extensions to non-algebraically-closed base fields are handled by base change arguments (Exercises 19.2.D/E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 0 curve with a rational point is P^1 (Proposition 19.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C has genus 0 and a k-rational (degree 1) point p, then C ≅ P^1_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: take L = O(p) of degree 1; h^0(L)=2 and the two sections give a closed embedding into P^1, forcing an isomorphism. Use when classifying genus 0 curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every genus 0 curve is a plane conic (19.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any genus 0 curve C admits a degree 2 very ample line bundle (ω_C^∨), giving a closed embedding into P^2 as a conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take L = ω_C^∨ (degree 2) and use the degree ≥ 2g+1/2g thresholds (here deg=2) to embed into P^2; thus genus 0 curves are conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-1 line bundle on non-P^1 curve has at most one section (19.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is not isomorphic to P^1_k and L has degree 1, then h^0(C, L) < 2 (i.e., at most one section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two independent sections existed they'd give a degree-1 morphism to P^1 hence an isomorphism; thus degree-1 line bundles detect P^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of degree-1 line bundles (19.4.2 corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: For C not isomorphic to P^1_k and degree-1 points p,q, O_C(p) ≅ O_C(q) iff p = q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from previous proposition: two different degree-1 points would produce two independent sections contradicting h^0<2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical geometric consequences (Pappus, Pascal) via linear series (19.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical theorems (Pappus, Pascal) can be derived by viewing configurations as divisors/linear series on plane curves/conics and applying previous separation/intersection arguments (Bezout, Cayley–Bacharach type statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intersection theory and divisor-counting on curves; the text sketches how degenerations of conics/linear series yield Pappus as a special case of Pascal.
